definition:
Repentance is turning back to God. It includes sorrow for sin, but it is more than regret: it is a change of mind that becomes a change of direction, away from sin and toward the God who has been offended and who offers mercy. Forgiveness is God's side of that turning. He releases the guilty from the debt of their sin, removes it, and restores them to himself, freely and at great cost to himself. Scripture keeps the two together from the prophets' “Return to Me, and I will return to you” (Malachi 3:7) to the risen Jesus' commission that “repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations” (Luke 24:47). And it adds a third thing: those who have been forgiven are to forgive. Repentance and faith are two sides of one turning (faith has its own study), and the ground of forgiveness, Christ's death, is treated in the study of the atonement.

The Old Testament's main word is shuv, ‘to turn, to return’, one of the commonest verbs in the Hebrew Bible (over a thousand times); most uses are ordinary movement, and the prophets make it the word for coming back to God. A second verb, nicham, means ‘to be sorry, to relent, to be comforted’, and it is used of God himself relenting from threatened judgment (Jonah 3:10). Forgiveness has several words: salach, ‘to forgive, to pardon’, which in the Old Testament always has God as its subject; nasa', ‘to lift, to carry away’ (Exodus 34:7); and kipper, ‘to make atonement’. The New Testament uses metanoeō, ‘to repent’ (34 times), and metanoia, ‘repentance’ (22 times). The words are built from ‘change’ and ‘mind’, but their meaning comes from use rather than from their parts, and in the Gospels and Acts they carry the full weight of the Hebrew shuv; the verb epistrephō, ‘to turn’, stands beside them (Acts 3:19). Metamelomai, ‘to regret’, describes Judas's remorse (Matthew 27:3). For forgiveness the chief verb is aphiēmi, ‘to release, let go, cancel’, and the noun aphesis, ‘release’, the word the Greek Old Testament used for the release of the Jubilee year (Leviticus 25:10).
ot:
The first sinners hide, and the first word God speaks to them is a question, “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). From that point the Bible's story is about a God who seeks and a people who must turn. Genesis ends with an act of human forgiveness: Joseph's brothers beg pardon for selling him, and Joseph, weeping, answers, “Am I in the place of God?” (Genesis 50:19), refusing revenge because God has turned their evil to good. At Sinai the pattern is set for Israel. After the golden calf, Moses intercedes and offers himself for the people (Exodus 32:30-32), and God reveals his name as “compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, maintaining loving devotion to a thousand generations, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin” (Exodus 34:6-7), while still refusing to call guilt innocence. The sacrificial system gave forgiveness a place and a cost. On the Day of Atonement the high priest confessed Israel's sins over a goat that carried them away into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:21-22), and forgiveness was pronounced through sacrifice. After the rebellion at Kadesh, God answers Moses' plea, “I have pardoned them as you requested” (Numbers 14:20).

The covenant itself anticipated failure and return. Leviticus 26:40-42 and Deuteronomy 4:29-31 and 30:1-10 foresee Israel in exile and promise that if the people return to the LORD with all their heart, he will return them to the land. Deuteronomy also promises that God will do what Israel cannot: “The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts” (Deuteronomy 30:6). Solomon's prayer at the temple dedication asks God to hear exiles who “come to their senses” and “repent” (1 Kings 8:47), where the Hebrew for both is built from shuv. The story of David shows the personal shape of repentance. Confronted by Nathan after his adultery and murder, he says, “I have sinned against the LORD,” and Nathan answers, “The LORD has taken away your sin” (2 Samuel 12:13), though the consequences in David's household remain. Psalms 32 and 51 turn that experience into prayer: the misery of hidden sin, the relief of confession, and the plea, “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10). Repentance here is not a payment. “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit” (Psalm 51:17), and forgiveness is the gift of a God with whom “there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared” (Psalm 130:4).

The prophets made ‘return’ their summons. Isaiah called Judah to cease doing evil and learn to do right, promising that sins like scarlet would be white as snow (Isaiah 1:16-18), and to return to the LORD, since “He will freely pardon” (Isaiah 55:7). Jeremiah, preaching in the decades before Jerusalem fell in 587 or 586 BC, repeats the word shuv more than any other book, sometimes with painful wordplay: ‘Return, faithless ones’, where ‘faithless’ is itself built from the same root (Jeremiah 3:14, 22). Ezekiel, among the exiles in Babylon, insists that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and pleads, “Turn! Turn from your evil ways! For why should you die, O house of Israel?” (Ezekiel 33:11). Hosea gives the words to pray (Hosea 14:1-2), and Joel asks for inward repentance, “rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2:13). The prophets also expose false repentance: a quick show of devotion that vanishes like morning dew (Hosea 6:4), or fasting joined to oppression (Isaiah 58:3-7). Yet they see that Israel's turning depends finally on God's gift of a new heart (Jeremiah 31:33-34; Ezekiel 36:26), and Jeremiah's new covenant ends with the promise, “I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more” (Jeremiah 31:34).

Two more notes complete the Old Testament picture. First, repentance is open to the nations. Jonah preached to Nineveh, the capital of Israel's enemy Assyria, and when the city turned from violence, God relented (Jonah 3:8-10); Jonah's complaint is that he knew God would, because he is “a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion” (Jonah 4:2), quoting Exodus 34. Jewish synagogues still read Jonah on the afternoon of the Day of Atonement. Second, the Scriptures speak of God ‘relenting’ (nicham), as when he announces judgment on a nation and then spares it if it turns (Jeremiah 18:7-8). Interpreters explain this language in different ways, but they agree that it teaches God's threats are meant to bring people back, not to seal their fate. Micah sums up the Old Testament's hope in a question, “Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity” (Micah 7:18), and a promise, “You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea” (Micah 7:19).
nt:
The New Testament opens with a call to turn. John the Baptist preached “a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins” (Mark 1:4) and demanded fruit to match it (Matthew 3:8), which for tax collectors meant honest collecting and for soldiers meant no extortion (Luke 3:10-14). Jesus took up the same call, “Repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15), and joined it to the arrival of God's kingdom. He said he had come to call not the righteous “but sinners, to repentance” (Luke 5:32), warned that without repentance all would perish (Luke 13:3, 5), and told three parables of lost things found (Luke 15), where heaven rejoices “over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:7). In the story of the younger son, repentance begins when he “came to his senses” and goes home with a confession, but the father runs to meet him before the speech is finished (Luke 15:17-24). Zacchaeus shows repentance as restitution, repaying fourfold what he had taken (Luke 19:8). Jesus also claimed the authority to forgive sins himself, which his critics rightly saw as a claim reserved for God (Mark 2:5-7).

Jesus bound divine forgiveness to human forgiveness. The prayer he taught asks, “forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors” (Matthew 6:12), and he adds that those who refuse to forgive will not be forgiven (Matthew 6:14-15). When Peter asks whether seven times is enough, Jesus answers “seventy-seven times” and tells of a servant forgiven a vast debt who throttles a fellow servant over a small one (Matthew 18:21-35). Luke records the instruction to rebuke a brother who sins and to forgive him if he repents, even seven times in a day (Luke 17:3-4), and from the cross Jesus prays, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). The Gospels also set two failures side by side: Judas, filled with remorse (metamelomai), returns the silver and takes his own life (Matthew 27:3-5), while Peter, who denied Jesus three times, is restored by three questions and a commission (John 21:15-17). The difference is not the size of the sin but where each man turned.

After the resurrection, repentance and forgiveness become the apostles' message to the world (Luke 24:47). At Pentecost Peter tells the crowd, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins” (Acts 2:38), and later, “Repent, then, and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped away” (Acts 3:19). Acts presents repentance both as a command and as a gift: God exalted Jesus “to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel” (Acts 5:31), and when Gentiles believed, the church concluded, “God has granted even the Gentiles repentance unto life” (Acts 11:18). In Athens Paul announced that God “now commands all people everywhere to repent” (Acts 17:30), and he summarized his preaching as “repentance to God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 20:21), calling for “deeds worthy of their repentance” (Acts 26:20).

The letters address repentance within the church. Paul says God's kindness is meant to lead to repentance (Romans 2:4), and he distinguishes “godly sorrow,” which brings repentance and salvation, from “worldly sorrow,” which brings death (2 Corinthians 7:10). He urges a church to forgive and comfort a disciplined member lest he be overwhelmed by sorrow (2 Corinthians 2:7), and tells believers to forgive “just as in Christ God forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32; Colossians 3:13). James calls for mutual confession and prayer (James 5:16), and John promises, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9), after warning that anyone who claims to have no sin is deceived. Hebrews contains the hardest texts: it says it is impossible to restore to repentance those who have tasted the heavenly gift and then fallen away (Hebrews 6:4-6), and that Esau “could find no ground for repentance” (Hebrews 12:17). Interpreters read these as describing apostasy, a deliberate and settled repudiation of Christ, not the struggles of believers who still want to return; how they relate to the security of believers is treated in the study of perseverance. Peter explains the delay of Christ's return as God's patience, “not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). Revelation calls five of its seven churches to repent (Revelation 2 and 3) and records, with grief, that under judgment the rest of humanity “did not repent” (Revelation 9:20-21; 16:9). To the end, the door stands open and the call is to turn.

keyTexts.why: God proclaims his name after the golden calf: compassionate, gracious, forgiving iniquity, yet not calling the guilty innocent. Later Scripture quotes this confession again and again, from Joel to Jonah.
On the Day of Atonement the high priest confesses Israel's sins over a goat that carries them away. Forgiveness has a place, a confession, and a cost.
Moses foresees exile and promises restoration when Israel returns to the LORD, and promises that God himself will circumcise their hearts. Repentance and God's renewing gift are joined.
Nathan confronts David, David confesses, and his sin is taken away, though its consequences remain. The pattern of confession and forgiveness in a single life.
The Bible's great prayer of repentance: confession without excuse, a plea for cleansing and a new heart, and the offering of a broken and contrite spirit.
The wicked are called to forsake their way and return to the LORD, who will freely pardon. Repentance is an invitation grounded in God's mercy.
God takes no pleasure in anyone's death and pleads with Israel to turn and live. Repentance is personal and urgent, and the new heart is both commanded and, in Ezekiel 36, promised.
Rend your hearts and not your garments. Repentance is inward before it is outward, and it rests on the character of God confessed in Exodus 34.
Nineveh turns from violence and God relents, to the anger of his prophet. Repentance is open to Israel's enemies, and God's mercy is wider than his servants want.
Seventy-seven times, and the parable of the unforgiving servant. Those forgiven an unpayable debt are bound to forgive others from the heart.
The son who comes to his senses and the father who runs to meet him, and an older brother who will not join the feast. Repentance met by a welcome it did not earn.
The risen Jesus commissions his followers to proclaim repentance and forgiveness of sins in his name to all nations. The Old Testament's call becomes the church's message.
Peter calls the crowd at Pentecost to repent and be baptized for the forgiveness of sins and promises the gift of the Spirit.
Paul distinguishes godly sorrow that leads to repentance and salvation from worldly sorrow that leads to death, and describes the earnestness true repentance produces.
Believers who confess their sins find God faithful and just to forgive, because Jesus Christ is their advocate and the atoning sacrifice. Repentance is part of ongoing Christian life.

history:
Jewish tradition gave repentance (teshuvah, from shuv) a central place. The Mishnah (compiled around AD 200) teaches that the Day of Atonement atones for sins against God, but that sins against another person are not atoned until the wronged person has been reconciled (m. Yoma 8:9), and Maimonides, in the Laws of Repentance in his Mishneh Torah (completed around 1180), described complete repentance as refraining from the sin when the same opportunity returns. The early church faced a practical question at once: what of Christians who sinned gravely after baptism? The Shepherd of Hermas (second century) announced one further opportunity for repentance. Tertullian's On Repentance (around 200 to 206) allowed a single public penance after baptism, though later, as a Montanist, he attacked a bishop who readmitted adulterers. When the Decian persecution (250) led many Christians to sacrifice to the gods, Cyprian of Carthage wrote On the Lapsed (251) and supported readmitting them after penance, while Novatian at Rome refused and formed a rigorist church. The Council of Nicaea (325, canon 8) set terms for receiving Novatian clergy back, and the church's mainstream held that no sin is beyond forgiveness for the one who repents. Early penance was public and lengthy; from the sixth century Irish monks spread private, repeatable confession guided by penitential books.

The medieval West organized repentance as the sacrament of penance. Peter Lombard's Sentences (written in the 1150s) counted it among seven sacraments and named its parts as contrition, confession, and satisfaction, and the Fourth Lateran Council (1215, canon 21) required every Christian of age to confess to a priest at least once a year. The Vulgate rendered Jesus' ‘repent’ in Matthew 4:17 with poenitentiam agite, which could be heard as ‘do penance’. Erasmus, in the Latin translation and notes that accompanied his Greek New Testament from 1516, argued that the Greek meant a change of mind or coming to one's senses. Martin Luther's Ninety-Five Theses, posted on 31 October 1517 against the sale of indulgences, open by saying that when Christ called people to repent he meant the whole life of believers to be one of repentance. The Augsburg Confession (1530, Article XII) defined repentance as contrition, the terror of conscience at sin, together with faith that sins are forgiven for Christ's sake, with good works following, and Luther's Small Catechism (1529) describes baptism as meaning that the old self is drowned daily through contrition and repentance. John Calvin (Institutes 3.3, 1559) taught that repentance follows faith and is produced by it, and defined it as a real turning of life to God that consists in the dying of the old nature and the coming alive of the new, lasting the whole of life. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563, Questions 88 to 90) uses the same two movements, and the Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 15, ‘Of Repentance unto Life’) calls repentance an evangelical grace, necessary for all, yet never a satisfaction for sin or a cause of pardon. The Council of Trent's fourteenth session (25 November 1551) reaffirmed penance as a sacrament with contrition, confession, and satisfaction as the acts of the penitent, and distinguished perfect contrition, sorrow out of love for God, from imperfect contrition or attrition, sorrow arising from fear of punishment, which disposes a person to receive grace in the sacrament.

After the Reformation, repentance remained a pastoral preoccupation. The Puritan Thomas Watson's The Doctrine of Repentance (1668) distinguished true repentance from its counterfeits. John Wesley, in The Scripture Way of Salvation (1765) and The Repentance of Believers (1767), taught a repentance before justification, a conviction of sin wrought by grace, and a continuing repentance of believers for the sin that remains in them. In the Orthodox churches confession is one of the holy mysteries, understood above all as healing, and the season of Great Lent is shaped by prayers of repentance such as the Great Canon of St Andrew of Crete. In the twentieth century Dietrich Bonhoeffer's Discipleship (1937) warned against ‘cheap grace’, which he described as forgiveness preached without repentance and grace without discipleship, and the Second Vatican Council prompted the revised Catholic Rite of Penance (1973), now usually called the sacrament of reconciliation.

differ.view: Repentance as the fruit of regeneration and faith (Reformed)
differ.body: Reformed theology teaches that repentance is an evangelical grace, God's gift and not a human work that earns pardon. The Spirit regenerates the sinner, and faith and repentance arise together as the first acts of the new heart; Calvin held that repentance follows faith and is produced by it, since only one who has seen God's mercy can truly hate sin and turn to him. Repentance consists in dying to the old self and coming alive to God, and it continues for the whole of life. It is necessary for all, since no one may expect pardon without it, but it is never a satisfaction for sin (Westminster Confession 15). Defenders point to Acts 5:31 and 11:18, where God grants repentance, to 2 Timothy 2:25, and to Ezekiel 36:26, and hold that this keeps both God's grace and the reality of repentance intact. Many Baptists and Presbyterians hold this view.

differ.view: Contrition and faith, law and gospel (Lutheran)
differ.body: Lutherans teach that repentance has two parts: contrition, the terror of conscience that God's law produces when it exposes sin, and faith, which the gospel creates when it announces forgiveness for Christ's sake. Good works follow as fruit. The law must be preached so that sinners know their need, and the gospel must be preached so that the terrified are comforted, and the two must not be confused. Repentance is a daily return to baptism, in which the old self is drowned and a new self arises. Lutherans also retain private confession and absolution as a gift, not a requirement for listing every sin, in which the pastor's word of forgiveness is God's own word. Defenders point to Romans 3:20 and 7:7 on the law's work, to Jesus' first call in Mark 1:15, and to Luther's first thesis.

differ.view: Repentance before faith and repentance of believers (Wesleyan)
differ.body: Wesleyan theology teaches that prevenient grace awakens the sinner to see his guilt and helplessness, and that this repentance, a conviction of sin with a readiness to turn from it, ordinarily comes before justifying faith as the way God prepares the heart, though it earns nothing and faith alone is the condition of justification. After justification there is a second repentance, the believer's growing awareness of the sin that still remains, which leads toward entire sanctification. Grace can be resisted, so the call to repent is a real call to a real response. Defenders point to the order of Mark 1:15 and Acts 20:21, to Jesus' teaching that sinners are called to repentance, and to Wesley's sermons of 1765 and 1767.

differ.view: The sacrament of penance or confession (Catholic and Orthodox)
differ.body: Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold that Christ gave his apostles authority to forgive and retain sins (John 20:22-23; Matthew 16:19; 18:18), and that sins committed after baptism are forgiven through a sacrament. In Catholic teaching the penitent brings contrition, confession of all grave sins to a priest, and satisfaction or penance, and the priest pronounces absolution in Christ's name; the sacrament restores grace lost through mortal sin and heals the wounds of lesser sins. Perfect contrition arising from love for God already obtains forgiveness when joined to the intention to confess. The Orthodox speak of confession as a mystery of healing more than a tribunal, with the priest as a witness and physician rather than a judge, and they avoid the Western categories of satisfaction. Both point to James 5:16 and to the early church's practice of public penance.

differ.view: Repentance and the free grace debate (evangelical)
differ.body: Among evangelicals the lordship and free grace controversy also concerns repentance. Lordship theologians hold that repentance, a genuine turning from sin to God, is inseparable from saving faith and is required in the gospel call (Acts 2:38; 17:30; 20:21), so that a faith with no turning is not saving faith. Free grace theologians differ among themselves. Some, such as Charles Ryrie, defined repentance in evangelism as a change of mind about Jesus that is included in believing. Others, such as Zane Hodges, held that repentance is not a condition of eternal life at all, pointing out that John's Gospel, written that readers might believe and have life, never uses the word, and taught that repentance restores fellowship with God and averts temporal judgment. Both sides affirm that God calls every believer to turn from sin.

errors:
The church has rejected distortions on both sides. Rigorism, represented by the Montanists and by Novatian, held that some sins committed after baptism could not be forgiven by the church; the church answered that no sin is too great for the mercy of God to the one who repents, and the unforgivable sin of Mark 3:29 has generally been understood as a settled, hardened rejection of the Spirit's witness to Christ, not a single failure a troubled believer fears he has committed. The opposite distortion makes repentance a payment. When penance came to be understood as buying off punishment, and indulgences were sold for money, the Reformers protested, and Protestants and Catholics now agree that no act of the penitent merits forgiveness, which is God's free gift grounded in the death of Christ. Repentance is also not the same as remorse. Judas regretted what he had done, and Paul warns that worldly sorrow, sorrow that looks only at itself, brings death (2 Corinthians 7:10). Nor is it a single emotional crisis that need never be repeated; Scripture treats it as the ongoing posture of the believer (1 John 1:8-9).

Forgiveness has its own distortions. It does not mean pretending that a wrong was not wrong, which is why God forgives while refusing to call the guilty innocent (Exodus 34:7). It does not require a victim to return to danger or to hide a crime from those charged with justice, and it is not the same thing as trust or reconciliation, which need the offender's repentance and time to rebuild (Luke 17:3). Finally, the church has rejected ‘cheap grace’, forgiveness announced without any call to turn, which leaves people unchanged and assured.
life:
Repentance gives a person somewhere to go with the truth about himself. Without it, sin can only be hidden, excused, or despaired over, and Psalm 32 describes what hiding does to the body and spirit. With it, sin can be named and handed over, because the God to whom one turns is “gracious and compassionate” and has already made provision for forgiveness in Christ. That is why the Bible's calls to repent are almost always paired with promises: return, and I will return to you. Repentance is not self-punishment, and it does not require a sinner to feel sorry enough before God will listen. It is turning around, and the father in Jesus' parable runs to meet the son before he has finished his speech. Repentance is also concrete: John the Baptist told tax collectors to stop cheating, and Zacchaeus paid people back. It often means apology, restitution, and changed habits, as well as prayer.

Forgiveness received becomes forgiveness given. Jesus taught his followers to pray for forgiveness in the same breath as they forgive, and he warned that a heart that will not release others has not grasped what it was released from. Forgiving is often slow, especially after deep harm, and it is not the same as forgetting, excusing, or restoring trust. It is the decision to give up the claim to repay, and to hand the wrong to God, who judges justly (Romans 12:19). Communities that practice confession and forgiveness, among spouses, families, and churches, can tell the truth to one another without being destroyed by it, and people who have been forgiven much, as Jesus said of the woman in Simon's house, tend to love much (Luke 7:47).
questions: David's sin was forgiven, yet its consequences remained in his family (2 Samuel 12). How does that distinguish forgiveness from the removal of consequences, and why does the difference matter?
Judas and Peter both failed Jesus on the same night. What does the New Testament show about the difference between remorse and repentance?
Jesus ties our forgiveness of others to God's forgiveness of us (Matthew 6:12-15; 18:21-35). What makes forgiving so hard, and what in the gospel makes it possible?
